content: Cresols are organic compounds classified as methylphenols, which belong to the group of aromatic organic compounds known as phenols. These compounds can exist as either solids or liquids depending on the temperature, as their melting points are close to room temperature. When exposed to air for extended periods, cresols undergo slow oxidation, which often results in a yellowish to brownish-red discoloration due to impurities. Cresols emit an odor characteristic of simple phenols, often described as resembling a medicinal smell. From a chemical perspective, a cresol molecule consists of a methyl group attached to the benzene ring of a phenol molecule. There are three structural isomers of cresols, each with the molecular formula (CH3)C6H4(OH): ortho-cresol (o-cresol), meta-cresol (m-cresol), and para-cresol (p-cresol). These isomers can exist individually or as mixtures. Cresols have a variety of applications. They are used as solvents for dissolving other chemicals, as disinfectants, and as deodorizers. Additionally, they are employed in the production of specific chemicals designed to eliminate insect pests. Cresol solutions are commonly used in household cleaning products and disinfectants, with Lysol being a well-known example. Historically, cresol solutions were utilized as antiseptics in surgical procedures, but their use in this capacity has largely been replaced by less toxic alternatives. In mid-20th century America, Lysol was also marketed as a disinfecting vaginal douche. Cresols are naturally present in various foods, as well as in wood and tobacco smoke, crude oil, coal tar, and wood preservatives such as creosote, cresolene, and cresylic acids. In the environment, small organisms in soil and water produce cresols as they break down organic materials. Xylenols, which are dimethylphenols, can be considered as derivatives of cresols with an additional methyl group. Inhalation of high concentrations of cresols over a short period can irritate the nose and throat. Ingestion of high levels of cresols can lead to burns in the mouth and throat, abdominal pain, vomiting, kidney damage, and effects on the blood and nervous system. Skin contact with high concentrations of cresols can result in burns and damage to the kidneys, liver, blood, brain, and lungs. No studies in humans or animals have shown that cresols adversely affect reproductive ability. The effects of long-term ingestion or skin contact with low levels of cresols remain unknown.
